name: Tiwa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Joseph, U.V. & Robbins Burling. 2001. Tone correspondences among the Bodo languages. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 24(2): 41-55.
catalog_locator: p. 49 (section 'TIWA', pp. 47-50; Table 2 'Tiwa Tones' p. 48; continuation p. 50). Sealang scan of 15 (read as image).
catalog_quote: Two-syllable words can have one of four possible tone patterns, and our first conjecture was that each syllable could have either tone, making four possible combinations in all. It proved more revealing, however, to consider the tone to be a feature of the entire word, while recognizing that either tone can occur on either the first or the second syllable. This is reminiscent of the pattern of pitch-accent languages such as Japanese, where the pitch contour varies according to the location of accent (McCawley 1978) and, for that matter, it recalls the pattern of English stress, which can fall on any syllable of a word. Unlike Japanese and English, however, Tiwa has two possible tones, and either tone can occur on any syllable. Tiwa words, that is, are distinguished not only by the contrast in tones, but by a contrast in the position at which the tones occur. It would be possible to describe Tiwa as being characterized by accent as well as tone, and to say that the tone is attracted to the accented syllable. This seems only to introduce an extra and unneeded complication, however, and we will content ourselves with saying that the tone can appear on either syllable of a two-syllable word. As will be described just below, a tone can appear on any syllable of a three-syllable word as well.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each Tiwa word carries exactly one lexical tone (high-level or falling) linked to one lexically specified syllable, which may be any syllable of the word (4 patterns on disyllables, 6 on trisyllables); syllables before it are mid/neutral and the tone spreads rightward to the word end. The location is contrastive and not predictable by position (khûn-da 'post' vs khun-dâ 'hurry'); the authors note an accentual analysis (tone docks on an accented syllable) is possible but do not adopt it. No separate word stress is described.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; pre-tonal syllables are described as mid/neutral in pitch, post-tonal syllables share the tone.
new_statements.exceptions: 2006 monograph pp. 10-12: verb suffixes and locative/dative/genitive case markers are toneless and simply continue the word's tone; accusative, instrumental, plural and some other noun suffixes carry an inherent falling tone after high-toned stems; jing 'toward' takes the tone opposite to the preceding word; almost all monosyllables in final -s have falling tone; the first-syllable vs second-syllable falling-tone contrast has low functional load and even literate native speakers mark it inconsistently. (Second-hand via Wikipedia < Jose 2014: in disyllabic roots a syllable with aspirated/fricative onset attracts the falling tone; tone tends to shift rightward in running speech.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: the authors define the phonological word as the stretch bearing a single tone (2006 p. 10); data are citation forms and echo compounds from Hill Tiwa speakers at Umswai, Karbi Anglong (fieldwork April 1999). The system is culminative lexical tone with free, lexically contrastive position; 'pitch accent' is the closest catalog reading, alternatively 'tone language, no stress statement'.
new_statements.identity_note: Joseph & Burling's data (2001, 2006) and Dawson 2020 describe Hill Tiwa as spoken around Umswai, West Karbi Anglong (the variety of the Jose 2014 dictionary and standard orthography). Dawson notes the plains variety of Morigaon district (described by Jacquesson 2001) is 'quite different'; Glottolog tiwa1253 covers both, no separate dialect codes known to me.

sources.note: pp. 47-50 'TIWA': every word has exactly one of two tones (high level / falling); in polysyllables the tone may sit on any syllable, giving 4 patterns for disyllables and 6 for trisyllables; pre-tonal syllables mid/neutral, tone spreads rightward. p. 49 explicitly says Tiwa could be described as having accent as well as tone with the tone attracted to the accented syllable, but the authors decline that analysis as an unneeded complication. Position of tone is lexically contrastive; no stress rule given.

sources.citation: Dawson, Virginia E. 2020. Existential quantification in Tiwa: disjunction and indefinites. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley.
sources.note: Phonology sketch (ch. 2, pp. 10-12): 'Tiwa has two contrastive tones: high and falling. These tones are associated with a particular syllable in the word, and spread left-to-right', referring to Joseph & Burling 2001 and Joseph 2014; orthography marks the tone on its syllable. Nothing on stress.
